historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Z-drug hypnotics
history.scopeNote: Basis scope: zolpidem; zopiclone's initial screening purpose unresolved.

starting.description: Documented support is bounded to Kaplan's zolpidem branch: he recalls a 1978 request for a zopiclone-like compound and a structural-hybrid proposal based on the drugs' similar actions. Wermuth's 2006 profile-directed zopiclone account conflicts with his 2008 extensive/random-screening framing; the initiating zopiclone purpose remains unresolved.

inspiration.description: For the documented zolpidem branch, known synthetic-drug actions and Kaplan's proposed shared-receptor relationship motivated hybrid design. The initial zopiclone screening purpose remains disputed. This is broad biological inspiration, without a claim of natural-molecule ancestry or an established initiating clue for zopiclone.

steps.description: According to Wermuth's 2006 retrospective, after benzodiazepine anxiolytic and tranquilizing effects became known, Rhône-Poulenc searched for functionally similar compounds and obtained zopiclone. His 2008 screening classification leaves the exact initial screening objective and stages uncertain; neither account establishes the earliest assay sequence or chemical starting structure.

A 1972-priority patent disclosed the pyrrolopyrazine series and the structure assigned to zopiclone; it reported behavioral pharmacology for the series. The 1983 zopiclone study abstract later reported benzodiazepine-like pharmacological activity.
Kaplan recalls a 1978 request for a zopiclone-like compound, followed by physical comparison of drug models and a deliberate hybrid-design proposal written with George.

Kaplan and George patented an imidazopyridine series with 1980 priority; Kaplan identifies its compound 75 as zolpidem. A 1985 original-study abstract reports receptor binding and rat electrocorticographic effects of zolpidem.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and tested a distinct pyrrolopyrazine series; Wermuth's accounts differ in how the initial screening objective is framed. For the later branch, Kaplan reports comparing physical structures and proposing hybrids; the team pursued substituted imidazopyridines, including compound 75. The sources do not establish an exact discovery-stage optimization pathway or justify attributing all series-level patent test outcomes to either named compound.

circumstances.description: The particular planned stage was Kaplan's reported structural-hybrid project following the zopiclone-like request. This does not assert that every experimental finding was expected or resolve the initial objective of cyclopyrrolone screening.

limits: Cyclopyrrolone/zopiclone program motivation rests on Wermuth's retrospective; his 2006 and 2008 descriptions frame screening differently. The earlier patent discloses chemistry and series-level pharmacology but not the origin narrative. Do not claim that a receptor-binding assay was used at the start of the early-1970s program.

Imidazopyridine/zolpidem's 1978 inspiration rests on Kaplan's first-person retrospective. The patent corroborates a later series disclosure and named inventors, not the full recalled causal sequence or the distribution of intellectual credit.
The class-level judgment concerns the two assigned founding branches. It does not establish the origin of every other GABA-A hypnotic or of all later compounds.
conflicts: Wermuth's 2006 article explicitly describes a benzodiazepine-profile-directed search for zopiclone, whereas his 2008 chapter places zopiclone under extensive screening generally framed as lacking a prior hypothesis and labels its figure random screening. These are not independent accounts and may describe different stages or use terms inconsistently; the precise initial objective is unresolved, not evidence for design from scratch.

Kaplan disputes how the 2013 New Yorker article and other accounts distribute intellectual credit for zolpidem. The patent names both Kaplan and George; these materials do not independently resolve individual priority.

Wermuth summarizes a zolpidem screening search as early 1980s, whereas Kaplan dates his conceptual project to 1978. These may refer to distinct stages, but their exact reconciliation is unverified. Wermuth also combines early-1970s zopiclone discovery with binding-profile language; the 1972-priority patent describes behavioral tests but does not date a receptor-binding assay.
gaps: The 1978 Jeanmart–Cotrel synthesis report and 1979 Blanchard et al. zopiclone-binding report were located but not read. Later 1983 and 1985 pharmacology papers were read only as abstracts.

No contemporaneous narrative documenting the cyclopyrrolone program's first observation, chemical lead, exact screening objective or sequence, or selection experiment was obtained; the retrospective screening descriptions remain in tension.
Kaplan's described 1978 written project and associated original laboratory notes were not obtained; the patent does not independently establish the recalled conceptual sequence.
A complete resolution of personal credit, the chronology of specific binding assays, and later analogue-specific trajectories is outside this class collection.
